rationale: Surprise minimization is a useful formal description of some persistent, feedback-controlled systems, but it is not established that individual cells in metazoan development tune internal states to predict future stimuli in anything like the way nervous systems do. Developmental cells clearly regulate toward physiological set points, yet the free-energy account adds little tested mechanism beyond ordinary homeostasis and is often close to true by definition for any system that persists.

Multicellularity and complex morphology are well explained by adhesion, division of labor, predation, and ecological cooperation, not by cells performing greedy infotaxis to minimize surprise. Information-seeking foraging is a real algorithm in some motile organisms, but there is no evidence it is the driver of the origin of multicellular bodies.

Gap junctions do let neighboring animal cells share ions and small metabolites, so coupled cells can respond to some of the same signals. Treating that sharing as the binding mechanism that creates a larger unified Self overstates both the uniqueness of gap junctions, since nerves, hormones, and mechanics also couple tissues, and the psychological notion of a shared Umwelt.

Several volatile anesthetics reduce gap-junction conductance, and some alcohols used as junction blockers are sedative, but most clinical anesthetics act primarily on ligand-gated receptors and potassium channels rather than as gap-junction uncouplers. Plant immobilization by the same chemicals is a weak and controversial analogue of animal anesthesia, so the cross-kingdom 'most anesthetics' claim does not hold.

Slime molds show decoy-like and inconsistent choices, and some ant colonies have been reported to respond to illusory patterns, so a few rationality failures do appear outside brains. Those cases are narrow and do not show that swarms fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions as vertebrate brains.

Biological and neural organization does sit between isolation and total mixing: too little coupling leaves independent units, and unrestricted sharing erases modules, as seen in differentiation, synaptic gating, and the integration-segregation tradeoff. Calling the intermediate regime the unique condition for a new Self is a theoretical gloss, but the underlying balance is well supported.

Many tumors lose gap-junction coupling and behave more autonomously, and a few cancer-like phenotypes can be normalized by embryonic or bioelectric context. Cancer as a whole is not a reversible shrinking of a computational boundary: driver mutations, selection, and microenvironment make most cancers not reversible by restoring tissue signals.

Homeostasis, memory, prediction, and distributed networks are real grades of biological control, and nervous systems did elaborate older excitable-cell physiology. The specific story that agency scaled by successively adding those pieces under surprise minimization is a plausible sketch, not a demonstrated evolutionary sequence.

Regulative development and canalization buffer many perturbations, including some mutational ones, so embryos often reach a workable anatomy and thereby flatten parts of the fitness landscape. Extra digits that acquire muscle and vessels illustrate this, though calling morphogenetic goal-directedness a major evolutionary ratchet goes beyond the strength of the evidence.

Tadpoles with eyes implanted on the tail and innervating the spinal cord can perform simple visual discrimination, so visual behavior is not strictly hardwired to the normal brain target. 'See quite well' overstates a partial, condition-dependent result, and brains still have strong default wiring even while they can adjust.

Transient disruption of planarian bioelectric connectivity can yield double-headed worms that keep regenerating that anatomy without a change in genomic sequence, so pattern set points can be rewritten physiologically in that system. That this is a better general strategy for regenerative medicine than genetic repair remains an unproven proposal.

Voltage-gated channels and gap junctions form feedback loops with multiple stable membrane states, and transient currents can switch those states without any change in the genes encoding the channels. That is ordinary excitable-cell physiology, and the software metaphor is fair for this kind of state-dependent switching.

Opioid receptors are ancient and have roles in pain, stress, and immunity, but the addictive power of opiates is explained by reward circuitry and endogenous opioid signaling, not by a leftover drive to keep other cells nearby. Nothing in early multicellular models links opiate reinforcement to the origin of cell cohesion.

Expressing ion channels and gap junctions in a unicell would alter its electrical behavior but would not supply adhesion, differentiation, or a developmental program sufficient for a metazoan-like body. Dissolving an animal body by retuning bioelectric dynamics alone is likewise far beyond what those conductances control.

Electrical signaling contributes to regeneration or wound responses in some animals, plants, and bacterial biofilms, and slime molds are sensitive to certain neuroactive drugs. A consistent transcriptomic reliance on electrogenic proteins from biofilms through plant and limb regeneration is not established, and many regenerative programs are dominated by other pathways.

Non-neural tissues compute and decide in a physiological sense, but timescale is not the main difference between them and networks that support experience. Current neuroscience and philosophy of mind give no good reason to assign a pancreas a proto-consciousness comparable to even a simple neural circuit.

An evolutionary search over simulated soft bodies, followed by manual assembly of Xenopus epidermal and cardiac cells, did produce novel motile aggregates whose behavior matched design goals in reported cases. The pipeline works for this narrow class of constructs, with the manual steps the claim already notes.

For the deciliated, heart-muscle-driven constructs, upright animals were reported to move in the simulated direction, and flipping the design cut net displacement both in the model and in the dish. That orientation control is a specific, published comparison and is likely to be right in direction and approximate magnitude.

The inversion result is a real control: the same tissue moves well only in the designed orientation, which is evidence against a purely accidental match. Other unmodeled factors, especially ciliary flow and tissue remodeling, can still contribute, so morphology is a major cause rather than the whole explanation.

Motile frog-cell aggregates do push external particles into piles, and the same designs collect particles in the simulation. The behavior is a straightforward consequence of locomotion in a debris field, and it was observed both in silico and in vivo.

Pairs of these aggregates were reported to collide, stick briefly, and circle before separating, more strongly when cilia were left intact. Hydrodynamic coupling from cilia makes that interaction physically expected, and the qualitative observation is credible even if 'often' is not precisely quantified.

In a voxel simulation with randomly phased contractile cells, selection for net displacement reliably favors shapes and active-passive layouts that turn local jitter into coherent travel. That derandomization is a standard outcome of this kind of evolutionary search and matches the reported runs.

The built aggregates lack a nervous system, mix epidermal and cardiac progenitors, and still settle into a stable motile form, so cell-level sorting and cooperation are doing real work. Their competence explains self-repair and cohesion better than it explains the specific designed gait, which was imposed by geometry.

Cardiomyocytes couple electrically and spontaneously synchronize even when no one designs the coupling, and the frog-cell constructs showed coherent contractions that contributed to movement. Phase matching is the expected default of gap-junction-coupled cardiac cells, not an extra imposed program.

Embryonic amphibian aggregates are known to close small wounds, and the reconfigurable organisms were reported to seal lacerations while holding an imposed shape. Maintenance is only partial, because fine sculpted features smooth out, but the repair claim itself is well supported.

Designs evolved as if on land produced bounding gaits that transferred poorly, and adding a simple fluid drag plus random phase offsets kept simulated bodies against the substrate far more of the time, with the stated contact fractions. Those modeling changes are a plausible reason the second round matched the aquatic constructs better.

Reaggregated amphibian embryonic tissue rounds off and closes small gaps, while larger concavities can persist, so a minimum feature size near a tenth of a millimetre is credible. The exact 100 µm cutoff is a preliminary measurement on animal-cap explants and may not be a sharp universal threshold.

Multicellular animals are made of cells with some autonomous physiology, so many familiar minds are collectives in a loose sense. The universal claim fails for unicellular cognitive agents, whose molecular parts are not themselves agents, and 'no indivisible cognitive being' is a stipulation rather than a finding.

After decapitation, some trained planarians relearn a task in fewer trials once the head regenerates, which is consistent with a retained bias. Classic memory-transfer reports were not reliable, and the savings can be sensitization or peripheral state rather than a specific memory written onto the new brain.

Xenopus tadpoles with eyes placed on the tail and optic fibers routed into the spinal cord can still learn a simple light-color association. Success is limited to a subset of animals and easy tasks, so 'readily' and a general claim that minds adapt to any radical body plan overreach the data.

Comparative anatomy, development, and behavior show cognitive capacities grading from chemotaxis and simple circuits to large brains, without a demonstrated binary jump on the timescale of single organisms. Large functional gaps exist, but the evidence favors continua of mechanisms rather than sharp on-off transitions.

Choosing the level of description that best predicts and controls a system is a sound experimental criterion, in the same spirit as treating a system with the stance that earns its keep. Agency is not only an instrumental score, but for practical attribution the claim is largely right.

Published dynamical models of gene networks can store associations between stimuli, complete partial patterns, and generalize, in the formal sense that later responses depend on earlier paired inputs. That is a property of certain multistable or Hebb-like models, not a demonstration that real gene networks learn as nervous systems do.

Goals, memory that outlasts the parts, and a locus of reward are reasonable marks of an integrated agent and match how we already treat organisms versus their cells. They are a useful stipulated checklist, not a settled account of what a Self is, and many systems meet one mark without the others.

Ranking agents by how far in space and time their goals reach is a coherent comparative scheme, from chemotaxis to planning. Those scales do not by themselves draw the boundary of a Self, which also depends on integration, persistence, and which observer is asking.

Physiological stress responses do couple local errors to distant effectors, as in inflammation, hormonal axes, and wound signals that recruit cells that were not at the injury. That binding into one homeostatic loop is real at the organism scale; identifying it as the general mechanism that creates larger Selves is an extra interpretation.

Behavioral control reused older cell-signaling components, so some continuity between physiological regulation and movement is plausible. There is no strong evidence that spatial problem-solving is essentially the same capacity as metabolic or transcriptional control, merely pivoted into three-dimensional space.

Planarians in barium, a broad potassium-channel blocker, lose head tissue and can regenerate heads that then tolerate barium, with comparatively limited transcriptional change. 'Completely insensitive' and the reading that cells navigate transcriptional space to solve a stressor evolution never saw are stronger than the physiological result warrants.

Xenopus tadpoles whose facial organs are placed in the wrong positions tend to approach a normal frog face during metamorphosis, with tissues taking abnormal routes and sometimes overshooting. That supports a target-morphology component in craniofacial remodeling, alongside ordinary growth mechanics, not a fully unconstrained navigation.

A localized injury to a deer antler can be followed, after the antler is shed, by an extra tine at the corresponding site in a later cycle, a long-noted trophic memory. The anatomy can be rewritten without a germline mutation; calling it a rewritable pattern memory is a reasonable description of an incompletely understood local growth effect.

Blocking gap junctions or shifting ion-channel conductances in regenerating planarians reliably changes head number, including two-headed and headless forms, without editing the genome. Transient blockade can also push head shape toward anatomies typical of other planarian species, though those shapes are approximations rather than a full species transformation.

Planarians induced by a brief gap-junction block to regenerate two heads continue to regenerate two heads from fragments after the drug is gone, despite an unaltered genome. The altered target is stable across multiple rounds of cutting, and it can be reset by a counteracting bioelectric treatment, which supports a physiological rather than genetic store.

In planarians, a transient voltage or gap-junction perturbation can reset the anatomical pattern that later regenerations follow, which is fairly called a rewritten pattern memory in that system. Evidence that the same mechanism is a conserved way to write false target morphologies across animals is much thinner.

In polyploid newt larvae, kidney tubules keep a normal lumen when cells are enlarged by using fewer cells in cross-section, and in the most extreme cases a single cell wraps to form the tubule. Different cell behaviors are recruited to the same anatomical outcome, which is a classic and well-reproduced result.

Injury to one Xenopus limb produces a rapid bioelectric change that can be imaged in the contralateral limb on a timescale of seconds. The signal is real and somewhat location-specific, but likening it to mirror neurons and a full somatotopic map overstates a propagating physiological response.

Ion channels, connexins, and some neurotransmitter pathways already function in both morphogenesis and nervous-system plasticity, and developmental-gene studies often recover 'neural' genes. A further specific overlap, large enough that memory genes characteristically show up in cancer and regeneration screens beyond that shared machinery, is plausible but not yet a demonstrated result.

Tissues respond to nutrients, injury, and some neurochemicals, but there is no evidence that developing or regenerating anatomy can be trained by reward and punishment toward an arbitrary morphological goal. The prediction remains untested, and ordinary growth control does not amount to reinforcement learning.

Because many channels and gap junctions are themselves voltage-sensitive, a brief depolarization can trigger regenerative potential change or junction closure and leave the circuit in a new regime. Those dynamical memories are standard in excitable cells and do not require a change in channel protein inventory.

Current and small molecules crossing a gap junction carry no molecular tag of which cell originated them, so coupling does blur some cell-level informational boundaries. That fact supports physiological integration; it does not by itself create a larger Self or guarantee pursuit of common goals.

Connexin loss and gap-junction closure often accompany carcinogenesis, and many connexins can suppress tumors, but closure is neither necessary nor sufficient for transformation. Cells in a tumor do act more autonomously; describing cancer as a return to unicellular selves caused by that closure is an over-unified reading of a multi-hit disease.

In Xenopus embryos, forcing a bioelectric state can push melanocytes toward a melanoma-like conversion on a wild-type background, and normalizing voltage or coupling can suppress tumor-like structures driven by strong oncogenes. Those embryo results are real, but they are not metastatic melanoma in the clinical sense and do not show that genetic change is generally unnecessary to cause or revert cancer.

Voltage-gated channels and slow bioelectric signaling long predate neurons and already operate in development and behavior of animals that lack or barely have nervous systems. The idea that morphogenetic control by analog bioelectricity came first, and fast spiking for locomotion later, fits comparative physiology, even though the historical handoff is inferred rather than observed.

Many ion-channel families are older than animals, and voltage-gated channel diversity does expand around the origin of metazoans with more complex body plans. The match is only partial, because context-sensitive channels also occur in unicellular relatives that lack those body plans, so phylogeny supports a continuum more than a tight tracking.

Misexpressing a single ion channel in Xenopus can induce ectopic eye tissue, including in posterior and non-head regions, by shifting a local voltage pattern upstream of eye genes. Those structures can be remarkably complete, but master regulators such as Pax6 also induce ectopic eyes in vertebrates, so the contrast that voltage succeeds where Pax6 cannot is only partly right.

Different ion-channel combinations can yield similar membrane voltages, and mutations in channels or connexins can change anatomy at a distance from the expressing cells, including coordinated shifts in fin form. Evolution is not free to swap channels without constraint, but electrogenic mutations are a real route to long-range morphological change.

When modules correct toward a target anatomy, some mutations that would displace a structure in a rigid system are phenotypically silent, which is the usual effect of developmental robustness and canalization. That shielding smooths parts of the fitness landscape; it does not neutralize the bulk of mutational harm.

Regulative development and regeneration are used constantly to repair injury, predation, and environmental damage, which are abundant selective pressures. Correcting mutational deviations may be a side benefit of the same machinery, but it is not a better candidate for the primary reason anatomical homeostasis exists.

Morphogenetic and transcriptional systems sense and act, but goal-directed physiology is not evidence of consciousness, even a minimal one. Mainstream theories tie experience to specific neural or informational organizations that these tissues have not been shown to possess.

Some general anesthetics inhibit gap junctions, and high doses of certain junction blockers sedate animals and arrest movement in Hydra and plants. Anesthesia is not in general gap-junction blockade, cells are not left as an intact healthy network whose only loss is a higher Self, and the primary targets are other membrane proteins.

A brief gap-junction block during planarian regeneration can produce head shapes resembling other planarian species, and after the drug is removed many fragments gradually remodel toward the species-typical head. The parallel with waking from anesthesia is metaphorical; the anatomical sequence itself is a reported and plausible finding.

Under a functional definition, simulations of dozens of published pathway models do show history-dependent responses that the authors classify as several memory types, including pairing and associative forms. Those are real dynamical behaviors of the equations, though several of the labels are much broader than memory in animals.

The biological pathway models were reported to express more of these history-dependent behaviors than random circuits matched for size and several centrality measures, with fewer models showing no memory. Matching on those statistics does not rule out every generic dynamical bias, but the comparison makes a purely arbitrary-network explanation less likely.

If a pathway is multistable, a patterned stimulus might in principle shift it without gene editing, so behavior-shaping is a coherent research idea. Nothing yet shows that stimulation schedules taken from these models can control real pathway function, drug resistance, or sensitization well enough to stand in for gene therapy.

Defining memory as a specific dependence of future behavior on past experience is the standard functional criterion and is deliberately substrate-independent. It is broad enough to include adaptation and hysteresis, but as a working definition that lets molecular networks be tested for trainability it is sound.

Memory-like responses were reported in all but four of the surveyed pathway models, and three of those four were tiny, which fits the idea that a handful of nodes rarely sustains distinct history-dependent modes. The inference that very small networks cannot have memory is too strong for a four-model remainder and a generous memory test.

Within this set of models, mean node count, edge count, degree, and hubness were reported not to correlate significantly with how much memory was scored. With only a few dozen networks that negative result is unsurprising and does not show that no topological feature is indicative.

Positive feedback with hysteresis, as in dual phosphorylation cycles of MAPK, is a known way for a biochemical network to hold a state after the stimulus ends. The claim correctly treats that architecture as conducive rather than necessary, since other nonlinearities can store history too.

In fixed ODE models, a stimulus pattern can move the system into a different basin so that a later neutral input is answered as if it had been paired, without any change to equations or parameters. That is ordinary multistability, and it is enough for the functional memory they define.

The surveyed models were reported to keep most of their scored memories when training pulses were scaled from tenfold to a hundredfold above baseline, with only a small fraction of models losing memories. Robustness across that wide range is plausible for saturating kinetics, though a few models forming more memories at weaker stimuli shows the result is protocol-dependent.

Adding noise was reported to preserve memories in most of these models and to raise the average memory count, especially for the associative test. Noise can stabilize switching in some nonlinear systems, but a general twenty-percent gain is a finding about this stimulation protocol and may not mean biological noise helps trainability.

Most of the models that showed unconditioned-stimulus memory were reported to keep the bulk of it over waits up to a hundred times the original interval, and a recall pulse usually did not erase it. Long retention is expected when the memory is a stable attractor, and the rare strengthening on recall is a minor extra.

Training a second associative pairing was reported to wipe out both associations in every biological and matched random model, whereas simpler unconditioned memories could be stacked. Catastrophic interference is expected in low-capacity dynamical stores, and the contrast between the two memory types matches that limitation.

The scored memories were spread across models drawn from bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals, with no obvious single taxon dominating. The sample per class is small, so an approximately even spread does not strongly show that proto-cognitive capacity is uniformly distributed across life.

A progressive drop of response across lengthening repeated stimuli, the operational test of habituation, was reported for at least one node pair in every testable pathway model, covering a few percent up to about half of pairs. Biochemical adaptation makes that low bar easy to meet, so universal occurrence in the 27 models is believable without implying clinical pharmacoresistance.

If biological models habituate on a larger share of node pairs than random circuits matched for coarse structure, selection could have enriched that behavior. The difference can also come from curated kinetics and feedback that the random ensemble lacks, so an evolved adaptation specifically for pharmacoresistance is not established.
